entries.zh: 天路無梯，望堯雲而不到。」
entries.en: yet the road to Heaven has no ladder, and though one gazes at the clouds of Yao, one cannot reach them."
entries.literal: the road to Heaven has no ladder; gazing at Yao's clouds one cannot arrive."

entries.zh: 昭宗覽之嘉歎。
entries.en: Emperor Zhaozong read the memorial and sighed in admiration.
entries.literal: Emperor Zhaozong read it and sighed in admiration.

entries.zh: 洎襲吉入奏，麵詔諭之，優賜特異。
entries.en: When Xiji presented the memorial in person, the emperor received him with a personal audience and lavished extraordinary gifts upon him.
entries.literal: When Xiji came in to present the memorial, the emperor addressed him face to face and bestowed exceptional favors.

entries.zh: 〈（《北夢瑣言》：習吉從李克用至渭南，令其入奏，帝重其文章，授諫議大夫，使上事北省以榮之。）〉
entries.en: (Northern Dreams, Trivial Tales: Xiji accompanied Li Keyong to Weinan and was sent to present a memorial at court. The emperor prized his prose, named him Remonstrance Grand Master, and had him report to the northern secretariat as a mark of honor.)
entries.literal: (Northern Dreams, Trivial Tales: Xiji followed Li Keyong to Weinan; the prince had him enter court with a memorial. The emperor valued his writings, appointed him Remonstrance Grand Master, and had him report to the northern secretariat to honor him.)

entries.zh: 其年十二月，師還太原，王珂為浮梁於夏陽渡，襲吉從軍，時笮斷航破，武皇僅免，襲吉墜河，得大冰承足，沿流七八里，還岸而止，救之獲免。
entries.en: That December, as the army marched back to Taiyuan, Wang Ke threw a pontoon bridge across the Xiayang ford and Xiji went with the column. The bridge cables snapped mid-crossing; the Martial Emperor barely escaped with his life. Xiji plunged into the river, caught a great slab of ice underfoot, and drifted seven or eight li downstream before he could claw his way ashore and be pulled out alive.
entries.literal: In the twelfth month of that year the army returned to Taiyuan; Wang Ke built a pontoon bridge at Xiayang Ford and Xiji followed the campaign. At the time the bridge cables broke and the crossing was destroyed; the Martial Emperor barely escaped. Xiji fell into the river, found a great floe of ice to bear his feet, drifted with the current seven or eight li, stopped when he reached the bank, and was rescued and spared.

entries.zh: 天復中，武皇議欲修好於梁，命襲吉為書以貽梁祖，書曰：
entries.en: During the Tianfu reign the Martial Emperor resolved to reopen relations with Liang and charged Xiji to draft a letter to the Liang Founder. It read:
entries.literal: In the Tianfu era the Martial Emperor deliberated on restoring good relations with Liang and ordered Xiji to draft a letter to the Liang Founder; the letter read:

entries.zh: 一別清德，十有餘年，失意杯盤，爭鋒劍戟。
entries.en: Since we parted in mutual regard, more than ten years have passed—shared cups turned to estrangement, and blades crossed in place of toasts.
entries.literal: Once we parted in pure virtue, more than ten years have passed; cups and dishes brought disappointment, and swords and spears vied in clash.

entries.zh: 山長水闊，難追二國之歡；
entries.en: Mountains lie between us and rivers run wide, so the old warmth of two allied states is hard to recover;
entries.literal: mountains stretch long and waters spread wide, hard to recover the joy of two states;

entries.zh: 雁逝魚沉，久絕八行之賜。
entries.en: the wild goose is gone and the fish lies sunk in the deep—your eight-line letters have long ceased to come.
entries.literal: wild geese have flown off and fish sunk deep, and for long the gift of an eight-line letter has been cut off.

entries.zh: 比者仆與公實聯宗姓，原忝恩行，投分深情，將期棲托，論交馬上，薦美朝端，傾向仁賢，未省疏闕。
entries.en: Not long ago we were bound by clan ties and I was unworthy of your kindness; we pledged our hearts to each other and looked to shelter under the same roof, struck up friendship in the saddle, praised each other at court, and leaned toward what was humane and worthy—I never thought you distant.
entries.literal: Of late your servant and you were in truth linked by clan name, and I was unworthy of your gracious conduct; we pledged deep affection and looked to shelter together, made friends on horseback, praised each other at court, and inclined toward the humane and worthy—I never perceived any neglect.

entries.zh: 豈謂運由奇特，謗起奸邪。
entries.en: Who could have foreseen that fate would take so strange a turn, and that slander would rise from the wicked?
entries.literal: Who would have said that fate arose from the strange, and slander rose from the wicked?

entries.zh: 毒手尊拳，交相於幕夜；
entries.en: Poisonous hands and clenched fists met under cover of night;
entries.literal: poisonous hands and honored fists were exchanged in the curtain of night;

entries.zh: 金戈鐵馬，蹂踐於明時。
entries.en: golden spears and iron horses trampled the bright age itself.
entries.literal: golden spears and iron horses trampled and trod in the bright age.

entries.zh: 狂藥致其失歡，陳事止於堪笑。
entries.en: Rash acts born of wine broke our good feeling; the incidents you cite are fit only for laughter.
entries.literal: Mad medicine caused the loss of good feeling; the matters set forth ended only in what could be laughed at.

entries.zh: 今則皆登貴位，盡及中年，蘧公亦要知非，君子何勞用壯。
entries.en: Now we both stand in high office and have reached middle age; even Duke Qu of old came to know his mistake—why should gentlemen still strain their prime?
entries.literal: Now we have all ascended to exalted rank and all reached middle age; even Duke Qu must know his error—why should a gentleman trouble to use his prime strength?

entries.zh: 今公貴先列辟，名過古人。
entries.en: You now outrank the feudal lords of the age, and your fame surpasses the ancients.
entries.literal: Now you are honored before the feudal lords of the age, and your fame surpasses the ancients.

entries.zh: 合縱連衡，本務家邦之計；
entries.en: Vertical alliances and horizontal leagues are fundamentally plans for house and state;
entries.literal: to ally vertically and join horizontally is fundamentally a plan for one's house and state;

entries.zh: 拓地守境，要存子孫之基。
entries.en: to expand territory and hold your borders is to preserve a foundation for your sons and grandsons.
entries.literal: to expand territory and guard borders is to preserve the foundation for one's sons and grandsons.

entries.zh: 文王貴奔走之交，仲尼譚損益之友，仆顧慚虛薄，舊忝眷私，一言許心，萬死不悔，壯懷忠力，猶勝他人，盟於三光，願赴湯火。
entries.en: King Wen prized friends who came running at his call; Confucius spoke of companions who could tell gain from loss. I know myself shallow and unworthy, yet I was once honored with your private regard; one pledged word bound my heart, and I would not repent though I died ten thousand deaths. My loyal strength still outmatches other men; I swear by sun, moon, and stars and would walk through fire and boiling water for you.
entries.literal: King Wen valued friends who ran on his errands; Confucius spoke of friends who could speak of gain and loss. Your servant looks back ashamed at his emptiness and shallowness, yet was once unworthy of your private favor; one word pledged the heart, and ten thousand deaths bring no regret. My stout breast of loyalty and strength still surpasses other men; I swear by sun, moon, and stars and am willing to walk through boiling water and fire.

entries.zh: 公又何必終年立敵，懇意相窺，徇一時之襟靈，取四郊之倦弊，今日得其小眾，明日下其危牆，弊師無遺鏃之憂，鄰壤抱剝床之痛。
entries.en: Why keep an enemy year on year, probing and testing, indulging a passing mood and draining the weary countryside—winning a skirmish today and storming a crumbling wall tomorrow—until broken armies leave arrows on the field and neighboring lands suffer the ruin the Book of Changes calls "the bed stripped bare"?
entries.literal: Why must you stand as enemy year after year, earnestly peering and probing, indulging a moment's temper and drawing on the weariness of the four suburbs—today gaining a small band, tomorrow taking down a perilous wall—so that a ruined army has no worry of leaving arrows behind and neighboring lands embrace the pain of the bed stripped bare?

entries.zh: 又慮悠悠之黨，妄瀆聽聞，見仆韜勇枕威，戢兵守境，不量本末，誤致窺覦。
entries.en: I fear too that loose tongues in your camp will mislead you: seeing me hoard strength and rest on my reputation, sheathe arms and hold my borders, they may mistake restraint for weakness and tempt you to covetous designs.
entries.literal: I also fear that idle factions will rashly pollute what reaches your ears, seeing your servant hide courage and rest on prestige, sheath arms and guard borders, and, without weighing root and branch, mistakenly provoke covetous glances.

entries.zh: 且仆自壯歲已前，業經陷敵，以殺戮為東作，號兼並為永謀。
entries.en: Moreover, long before my prime I was already plunging among enemies, treating slaughter as spring plowing and calling conquest my lasting design.
entries.literal: Moreover, from before my prime your servant has already plunged among enemies, taking slaughter as spring plowing and calling annexation his lasting plan.

entries.zh: 及其首陟師壇，躬被公兗，天子命我為群後，明公許我以下交，所以斂跡愛人，蓄兵務德，收燕薊則還其故將，入蒲阪而不負前言。
entries.en: When I first mounted the commander's altar and received the ducal regalia in person, the Son of Heaven named me among the feudal lords and you, Illustrious Lord, treated me as an equal friend; since then I have restrained my conduct and cherished my people, husbanded arms and pursued virtue, restored Yan and Ji's former commanders when I took those lands, and kept my word when I entered Puban.
entries.literal: When I first ascended the commander's altar and personally received the ducal regalia, the Son of Heaven ordered me as one of the feudal lords and you, Illustrious Lord, allowed me friendship as with an inferior; therefore I restrained my tracks and cherished men, stored up arms and pursued virtue, and when I took Yan and Ji I returned their former generals, and when I entered Puban I did not betray prior words.

entries.zh: 況五載休兵，三邊校士，鐵騎犀甲，雲屯穀量。
entries.en: For five years my armies have rested while the three frontiers drilled their men; iron cavalry and rhinoceros-hide armor stand massed like clouds, and grain is piled like hills.
entries.literal: Moreover, for five years arms have rested and the three frontiers have drilled soldiers; iron cavalry and rhinoceros-hide armor mass like clouds, and grain is heaped like hills.

entries.zh: 馬邑兒童，皆為銳將；
entries.en: The boys of Mayi are all seasoned commanders;
entries.literal: the boys of Mayi are all sharp commanders;

entries.zh: 鷲峰宮闕，鹹作京坻。
entries.en: the storehouses on Vulture Peak might as well be the capital's granary mound.
entries.literal: the palaces on Vulture Peak all serve as the capital's granary mound.

entries.zh: 問年猶少於仁明，語地幸依於險阻，有何覘睹，便誤英聰。
entries.en: Compare our years and I am still the younger; compare our terrain and I am blessed with natural barriers—what is there for you to reconnoiter that should mislead so keen a mind?
entries.literal: Ask about years and I am still younger than your humane clarity; speak of terrain and I am fortunate to rely on peril and obstruction—what is there to spy out that should mislead your brilliant discernment?

entries.zh: 況仆臨戎握兵，粗有操斷，屈伸進退，久貯心期。
entries.en: Moreover, I have stood at the head of armies and learned something of command; when to bend, when to strike, when to advance or pull back—these choices I have long weighed in advance.
entries.literal: Moreover, your servant faces battle and holds the army, and has some rough power of decision; bending and stretching, advancing and retreating, he has long stored these in his heart's intent.

entries.zh: 勝則撫三晉之民，敗則征五部之眾，長驅席卷，反首提戈。
entries.en: Victory would let me soothe the people of the Three Jins; defeat would still let me rally the Five Divisions; I could drive far and sweep all before me, then wheel about with spear in hand.
entries.literal: If victorious I will soothe the people of the Three Jins; if defeated I will levy the hosts of the Five Divisions; driving far in sweeping advance, I will turn my head and raise spear.

entries.zh: 但慮隳突中原，為公後患，四海群謗，盡歸仁明，終不能見仆一夫，得仆一馬。
entries.en: I only fear ravaging the Central Plain and leaving you a lasting trouble; the world's blame would fall on your reputation for humanity, and in the end you would not capture a single man or horse of mine.
entries.literal: I only fear ravaging and striking the Central Plain and making a later trouble for you; the slanders of the four seas would all fall on your humane clarity, and in the end you could not see a single man of mine or obtain a single horse of mine.

entries.zh: 銳師儻失，則難整齊，請防後艱，願存前好。
entries.en: If elite troops are once broken, they are hard to re-form; guard against later hardship, and let us keep the friendship we once had.
entries.literal: If sharp troops should be lost, they are hard to set in order again; I beg you to guard against later hardship and wish to preserve our former good feeling.

entries.zh: 矧復陰山部落，是仆懿親；
entries.en: To say nothing of the Yin Mountain tribes, who are my own close kin;
entries.literal: how much more the tribes of Yin Mountain, who are your servant's close kin;

entries.zh: 回紇師徒，累從外舍。
entries.en: the Uighur hosts have marched beside my house again and again.
entries.literal: the Uighur masters and disciples have repeatedly followed my outer household.

entries.zh: 文靖求始畢之眾，元海征五部之師，寬言虛詞，猶或得志。
entries.en: Wen Jing sought the hosts of Shibi; Yuan Hai marched the Five Divisions—with empty boasts they still sometimes won their way.
entries.literal: Wen Jing sought the hosts of Shibi; Yuan Hai levied the armies of the Five Divisions—with broad words and empty phrases they still sometimes achieved their aim.

entries.zh: 今仆散積財而募勇輩，輦寶貨以誘義戎，征其密親，啗以美利，控弦跨馬，寧有數乎！
entries.en: Today I scatter my hoarded wealth to recruit warriors, cart treasure to entice the frontier tribes, call up their close kin, and feed them rich reward—who can count the bowmen and horsemen I could field!
entries.literal: Now your servant disperses accumulated wealth to recruit bold fellows, carts treasure to entice the righteous barbarians, summons their close kin, feeds them with fine profit—bow in hand, astride horse, can there be any counting them!

entries.zh: 但緣荷位天朝，惻心疲瘵，峨峨亭障，未忍起戎。
entries.en: Only because I hold office under the Son of Heaven, my heart aches for a worn and afflicted people, and I cannot bear to raise arms along those towering frontier walls.
entries.literal: Only because I bear office under the heavenly court, my heart aches for the weary and afflicted, and the towering frontier posts—I cannot bear to raise arms.

entries.zh: 亦望公深識鄙懷，洞回英鑒，論交釋憾，慮禍革心，不聽浮譚，以傷霸業。
entries.en: I hope you will read my humble intent aright, turn your keen judgment, renew friendship and lay resentment aside, foresee disaster and change your course, and refuse idle talk that would wound your hegemony.
entries.literal: I also hope you will deeply know my humble heart, turn your brilliant mirror, discuss friendship and release resentment, consider disaster and change your mind, and not heed floating talk to harm your hegemonic enterprise.

entries.zh: 夫《易》惟忌滿，道貴持盈，儻恃勇以喪師，如擎盤而失水，為蛇刻鶴，幸賜徊翔，
entries.en: The Book of Changes warns against excess; the Way values holding one's gains. To lean on courage and lose an army is to carry a full tray and spill the water, or to carve legs on a snake—I beg you grant me room to turn aside,
entries.literal: The Changes warns only against fullness; the Way esteems holding fullness. If one relies on courage and loses the army, it is like carrying a tray and losing the water, or carving a crane on a snake—I beg you grant me circling flight,

entries.zh: 仆少負褊心，天與直氣，間謀詭論，誓不為之。
entries.en: I have been narrow-spirited since youth, yet Heaven gave me an upright temper; intrigue and crafty argument I swear never to practice.
entries.literal: your servant from youth has borne a narrow heart and Heaven gave him upright spirit; secret plots and crafty arguments he swears never to make.

entries.zh: 唯將藥石之譚，願托金蘭之分。
entries.en: I offer only words harsh as medicine, and ask to renew the bond we once called kin.
entries.literal: I will only offer talk harsh as medicine and stone, and wish to entrust myself to the bond of metal and orchid.

entries.zh: 儻愚衷未豁，彼抱猶迷，假令罄三朝之威，窮九流之辯，遣回肝膈，如俟河清。
entries.en: If my foolish heart cannot reach you and your mind stays closed, then even exhausting the prestige of three dynasties and every argument the nine schools know would not open your breast—it would be like waiting for the Yellow River to run clear.
entries.literal: If my foolish heart is not opened and your breast still deluded, even if one exhausted the prestige of three courts and exhausted the arguments of the nine schools, to send back the liver and diaphragm would be like waiting for the river to clear.

entries.zh: 今者執簡吐誠，願垂保鑒。
entries.en: Now, brush in hand, I speak plainly and beg your careful regard.
entries.literal: Now, holding the bamboo slip, I speak my sincerity and beg you to bestow your safeguarding mirror.

entries.zh: 仆自眷私睽隔，翰墨往來，或有鄙詞，稍侵英聽，亦承嘉論，每賜罵言。
entries.en: Since our private bond was broken, letters have flown back and forth; some of my words may have been coarse and grated on your ear, yet I have also received your fine replies—and your scolding, which I took as kindness.
entries.literal: Since private favor was divided, brush and ink have gone back and forth; sometimes coarse words have slightly offended your brilliant hearing, yet I have also received fine discourse and been repeatedly granted words of scolding.

entries.zh: 敘歡既罷於尋戈，焚謗幸蠲其載筆，窮因尚口，樂貴和心，願祛沉閼之嫌，以復塤篪之好。
entries.en: Shared joy gave way to drawn swords; let us burn the slanders and erase what the brush recorded. In hardship men still prize honest speech; in friendship they value harmony of heart. Remove the buried grudge between us and restore the old music of pipe and flute.
entries.literal: Joy in reunion has already ended in seeking spears; burning slander fortunately cancels what the brush recorded. In extremity one still esteems the mouth; in pleasure one values harmony of heart. I wish to remove the suspicion of deep blockage and restore the good accord of xun and chi.

entries.zh: 今者卜於嚬分，不欲因人，專遣使乎，直詣鈴閣。
entries.en: Reading the lines of discord in our faces, I will not send another man's words; I dispatch an envoy of my own straight to your command pavilion.
entries.literal: Now, divining on the lines of a frown, I do not wish to rely on another person; I specially send an envoy to go straight to your bell pavilion.

entries.zh: 古者兵交兩地，使在其間，致命受辭，幸存前誌。
entries.en: In antiquity, when two armies met, envoys passed between them at the risk of their lives; fortunately the old chronicles still preserve that precedent.
entries.literal: In antiquity when arms clashed between two regions, envoys stood between them, risking life to receive words—fortunately the former records survive.

entries.zh: 昔賢貴於投分，義士難於屈讎，若非仰戀恩私，安可輕露肝膈，淒淒丹愫，炳炳血情，臨紙向風，千萬難述。
entries.en: Worthies of old prized sworn fellowship; men of honor hate to bow to a feud. Had I not still yearned for your private kindness, how could I lay bare my inmost heart? My loyal breast is desolate, my feeling bright as blood; facing this page into the wind, words fail a thousand times over.
entries.literal: Former worthies prized pledging their portion; men of honor find it hard to bow to enmity. If not for looking up in longing for private favor, how could one lightly expose liver and diaphragm? My crimson heart is desolate, my bloody feeling bright; facing the paper toward the wind, a thousand myriad things are hard to tell.

entries.zh: 梁祖覽之，至「毒手尊拳」之句，怡然謂敬翔曰：「李公鬥絕一隅，安得此文士！
entries.en: The Liang Founder read the letter, and at the line "poisonous hands and honored fists" he said with pleasure to Jing Xiang, "Lord Li holds only a corner of the empire—where did he find a writer like this!
entries.literal: The Liang Founder read it, and when he came to the line "poisonous hands and honored fists," he said with pleasure to Jing Xiang: "Lord Li holds a corner of the realm in struggle—how does he obtain such a literary man!

entries.zh: 如吾之智算，得襲吉之筆才，虎傅翼矣！」
entries.en: If a mind like mine had Xiji's pen, it would be a tiger given wings!"
entries.literal: If my schemes had Xiji's brush talent, it would be a tiger given wings!"

entries.zh: 又讀至「馬邑兒童」、「陰山部落」之句，梁祖怒謂敬翔曰：「李太原殘喘餘息，猶氣吞宇宙，可詬罵之。」
entries.en: But when he reached "boys of Mayi" and "Yin Mountain tribes," the Founder turned angry and told Jing Xiang, "Li of Taiyuan is a man on his last breath, yet he still talks as if he could swallow the universe—answer him with abuse."
entries.literal: Reading further to the lines "boys of Mayi" and "Yin Mountain tribes," the Liang Founder said angrily to Jing Xiang: "Li of Taiyuan is a dying breath with remnants of life, yet still swallows the universe in his spirit—he can be reviled and scolded."

entries.zh: 及翔為報書，詞理非勝，由是襲吉之名愈重。
entries.en: Jing Xiang drafted the reply, but his prose could not match Xiji's; Xiji's reputation rose all the higher.
entries.literal: When Jing Xiang drafted the reply, its rhetoric and reasoning did not prevail; because of this Xiji's name grew still heavier.

entries.zh: 〈（《通鑒考異》引《唐末見聞錄》載全忠回書云：前年洹水，曾獲賢郎；
entries.en: (Zizhi Tongjian, Examination of Variants cites Late Tang Eyewitness Records: in his reply Quanzhong wrote, The year before last at the Huan River we captured your worthy son;
entries.literal: (Zizhi Tongjian, Examination of Variants cites Late Tang Eyewitness Records on Quanzhong's reply: The year before last at Huan River we once captured your worthy son;

entries.zh: 去歲青山，又擒列將。
entries.en: last year at Green Mountain we took your commanders again.
entries.literal: last year at Green Mountain we again took your ranked generals.

entries.zh: 蓋梁之書檄，皆此類也。）〉
entries.en: such was the tone of Liang's letters and proclamations.)〉
entries.literal: In general Liang's letters and proclamations were all of this sort.)〉

entries.zh: 襲吉在武皇幕府垂十五年，視事之暇，唯讀書業文，手不釋卷。
entries.en: Xiji served in the Martial Emperor's headquarters for nearly fifteen years; in whatever leisure his duties allowed he read and wrote without setting a book down.
entries.literal: Xiji was in the Martial Emperor's staff office for nearly fifteen years; in the leisure of handling affairs he only read books and pursued writing, his hand never leaving the scroll.

entries.zh: 性恬於榮利，獎誘後進，不以己能格物。
entries.en: He cared little for rank or gain, encouraged younger men, and never used his own talent to block others.
entries.literal: By nature he was indifferent to glory and profit, encouraged and guided juniors, and did not use his own ability to obstruct others.

entries.zh: 參決府事，務在公平，不交賂遺，綽綽有士大夫之風概焉。
entries.en: In council he strove for fairness, took no bribes, and bore himself with the ample dignity of a scholar-official.
entries.literal: In deliberating commandery affairs he strove for fairness, accepted no bribes or gifts, and had ample bearing of a scholar-official.

entries.zh: 天祐三年六月，以風病卒於太原。
entries.en: In the sixth month of Tianyou year three he died of a stroke at Taiyuan.
entries.literal: In the sixth month of the third year of Tianyou he died of wind illness at Taiyuan.

entries.zh: 同光二年，追贈禮部尚書。
entries.en: In Tongguang year two he was posthumously honored as Minister of Rites.
entries.literal: In the second year of Tongguang he was posthumously granted the office of Minister of Rites.

entries.zh: 王緘，幽州劉仁恭故吏也。
entries.en: Wang Jian had been a clerk in the service of Liu Rengong of Youzhou.
entries.literal: Wang Jian was a former clerk of Liu Rengong of Youzhou.

entries.zh: 少以刀筆直記室，仁恭假以幕職，令使鳳翔。
entries.en: As a youth he served as recorder in Rengong's secretariat; the lord gave him a staff post and sent him on a mission to Fengxiang.
entries.literal: In youth he served as recorder with brush and knife; Rengong lent him a staff post and sent him as envoy to Fengxiang.

entries.zh: 還經太原，屬仁恭阻命，武皇留之。
entries.en: On his return he passed through Taiyuan; Rengong had meanwhile defied the court, and the Martial Emperor detained him.
entries.literal: Returning he passed through Taiyuan; it happened that Rengong blocked his orders, and the Martial Emperor detained him.

entries.zh: 緘堅辭復命，書詞稍抗，武皇怒，下獄詰之，謝罪聽命，乃署為推官，曆掌書記。
entries.en: Jian insisted on returning to complete his mission; his letter was defiant in tone. The Martial Emperor in anger threw him into prison and questioned him. Jian apologized and submitted; he was named investigating officer and later chief secretary.
entries.literal: Jian firmly declined to return to his commission; his letter's wording was somewhat defiant. The Martial Emperor was angry, put him in prison and interrogated him; he apologized and obeyed orders, and was then appointed investigating officer and successively served as chief secretary.

entries.zh: 〈（《契丹國誌·韓延徽傳》：延徽自契丹奔晉，晉王欲置之幕府掌書記，王緘嫉之，延徽不自安，求東歸省母，遂復入契丹，寓書於晉王，敘所以北去之意。
entries.en: (Khitan State Records, Biography of Han Yanhui: Yanhui fled the Khitan for Jin; the Prince of Jin wished to make him chief secretary. Wang Jian resented him; uneasy in Taiyuan, Yanhui asked leave to visit his mother in the east, returned to the Khitan, and wrote the prince explaining why he had gone north.
entries.literal: (Khitan State Records, Biography of Han Yanhui: Yanhui fled from Khitan to Jin; the Prince of Jin wished to place him in the staff office as chief secretary. Wang Jian envied him; Yanhui was ill at ease, asked to go east to visit his mother, and thus re-entered Khitan. He sent a letter to the Prince of Jin explaining why he went north.

entries.zh: 且曰：「非不戀英主，非不思故鄉，所以不留，正懼王緘之讒耳。」）〉
entries.en: He wrote, "It is not that I do not love an enlightened master or long for home; I dare not stay because I fear Wang Jian's slander.")〉
entries.literal: He also said: "It is not that I do not cherish an enlightened lord, nor that I do not think of my homeland; the reason I do not stay is precisely that I fear Wang Jian's slander.")〉

entries.zh: 從莊宗經略山東，承製授檢校司空、魏博節度使。
entries.en: He followed Emperor Zhuangzong in the pacification of Shandong and received by imperial order the acting title Minister of Works and the post of military commissioner of Weibo.
entries.literal: Following Emperor Zhuangzong in pacifying Shandong, he received by imperial order appointment as Acting Minister of Works and military commissioner of Weibo.

entries.zh: 緘博學善屬文，燕薊多文士，緘後生，未知名，及在太原，名位驟達。
entries.en: Jian was erudite and a fine writer; Yan and Ji had many men of letters, and Jian as a younger man was still unknown—at Taiyuan his name and rank rose overnight.
entries.literal: Jian was broadly learned and skilled at composing text; Yan and Ji had many literary men. Jian was younger and not yet known by name; once he was at Taiyuan, fame and rank rose swiftly.

entries.zh: 燕人馬鬱，有盛名於鄉里，而緘素以吏職事鬱。
entries.en: Ma Yu of Yan enjoyed great local fame, though Jian had long served him in a clerk's capacity.
entries.literal: Ma Yu of Yan had great fame in his home district, while Jian had long served Yu in a clerk's post.

entries.zh: 及鬱在太原，謂緘曰：「公在此作文士，所謂避風之鳥，受賜於魯人也。」
entries.en: When Yu came to Taiyuan he told Jian, "You play the literary man here—the bird that flees the storm and finds shelter with a stranger in Lu."
entries.literal: When Yu was at Taiyuan he said to Jian: "You serve here as a literary man—the so-called bird that flees the wind and receives favor from the man of Lu."

entries.zh: 每於公宴，但呼王緘而已。
entries.en: At every public feast he would call only "Wang Jian" and use no other name for him.
entries.literal: At every public banquet he would only call out "Wang Jian" and nothing more.

entries.zh: 十年，從征幽州，既獲仁恭父子，莊宗命緘為露布，觀其旨趣。
entries.en: In the tenth year he marched on Youzhou; after Rengong and his sons were taken, Emperor Zhuangzong ordered Jian to draft the victory bulletin to see where his loyalties lay.
entries.literal: In the tenth year he followed the campaign against Youzhou; after Rengong father and son were captured, Emperor Zhuangzong ordered Jian to draft the victory bulletin to observe his intent.

entries.zh: 緘起草無所辭避，義士以此少之。
entries.en: Jian wrote the bulletin without hesitation or evasion, and men of honor thought less of him for it.
entries.literal: Jian drafted it without any evasion or refusal; men of honor therefore thought somewhat less of him.

entries.zh: 胡柳之役，緘隨輜重前行，歿於亂兵。
entries.en: At the battle of Huliu, Jian marched with the baggage train ahead of the column and was killed in the rout.
entries.literal: In the battle at Huliu, Jian followed the baggage train forward and perished among the disorderly troops.

entries.zh: 際晚，盧質還營，莊宗問副使所在，曰：「某醉不之知也。」
entries.en: Near evening Lu Zhi returned to camp; the emperor asked where the deputy commissioner was, and Lu said, "I was drunk and do not know."
entries.literal: Near evening Lu Zhi returned to camp; Emperor Zhuangzong asked where the deputy commissioner was, and he said: "I was drunk and do not know."

entries.zh: 既而緘凶問至，莊宗流涕久之，得其喪，歸葬太原。
entries.en: Word of Jian's death soon arrived; Emperor Zhuangzong wept a long while, recovered the body, and had it buried at Taiyuan.
entries.literal: Soon word of Jian's death arrived; Emperor Zhuangzong wept for a long time, recovered his coffin, and returned it for burial at Taiyuan.

entries.zh: 自廣明大亂之後，諸侯割據方面，競延名士，以掌書檄。
entries.en: After the great disorders of the Guangming reign, regional lords carved up the empire and competed to recruit famous scholars to draft their letters and battle proclamations.
entries.literal: From after the great disorder of the Guangming era, feudal lords held regions by force and vied to summon famous scholars to manage letters and proclamations.

entries.zh: 是時梁有敬翔，燕有馬鬱，華州有李巨川，荊南有鄭準，
entries.en: Liang had Jing Xiang, Yan had Ma Yu, Hua had Li Juchuan, and Jingnan had Zheng Zhun,
entries.literal: At that time Liang had Jing Xiang, Yan had Ma Yu, Hua Prefecture had Li Juchuan, and Jingnan had Zheng Zhun,

entries.zh: 〈（《唐新纂》云：鄭準，士族，未第時，佐荊門上穀蓮幕，飛書走檄，不讓古人，秉直去邪，無慚往哲，考準為成汭書記，汭封上穀郡王。）〉
entries.en: (New Tang Compendium: Zheng Zhun came from the gentry; before he passed the examinations he served on the lotus-staff of Shanggu at Jingmen, drafting dispatches that matched the ancients and upholding rectitude without shame before the sages of old. He served as secretary to Cheng Rui, who was enfeoffed as Prince of Shanggu.)〉
entries.literal: (New Tang Compendium says: Zheng Zhun, of the gentry class, before passing the examinations assisted the Shanggu lotus-staff office at Jingmen; in flying letters and running proclamations he yielded to no ancients, upheld rectitude and expelled evil without shame before former sages. Examined: Zhun was secretary to Cheng Rui, and Rui was enfeoffed as Prince of Shanggu Commandery.)〉

entries.zh: 鳳翔有王超，
entries.en: Fengxiang had Wang Chao,
entries.literal: Fengxiang had Wang Chao,

entries.zh: 〈（《北夢瑣言》：唐末，鳳翔判官王超，推奉李茂貞，挾曹、馬之勢，箋奏文檄，恣意翱翔。
entries.en: (Northern Dreams, Trivial Tales: Late in Tang, Fengxiang aide Wang Chao backed Li Maozhen and wielded power like Cao Cao and Sima Yi; his memorials and battle letters ranged freely wherever he chose.
entries.literal: (Northern Dreams, Trivial Tales: At the end of Tang, Fengxiang administrative aide Wang Chao promoted and supported Li Maozhen, wielding the power of Cao and Ma; in memorials and military documents he soared as he pleased.

entries.zh: 後為興元留後，遇害，有《鳳鳴集》三十卷行於世。）〉
entries.en: He later became acting commissioner of Xingyuan, was killed in the turmoil, and left the Phoenix Cry Collection in thirty juan.)〉
entries.literal: Later he became acting commissioner of Xingyuan and met with violent death; his Phoenix Cry Collection in thirty juan circulated in the world.)〉

entries.zh: 錢塘有羅隱，魏博有李山甫，皆有文稱，與襲吉齊名於時。
entries.en: Qiantang had Luo Yin and Weibo had Li Shanfu; all were famed for their writing and ranked with Xiji in that age.
entries.literal: Qiantang had Luo Yin, Weibo had Li Shanfu—all had literary fame and were ranked with Xiji in their day.

entries.zh: 十二年，莊宗定河朔，史建瑭收新鄉，敬義謁見。
entries.en: In the twelfth year Zhuangzong pacified Hebei; when Shi Jiantang took Xinxiang, Jingyi came to pay his respects.
entries.literal: In the twelfth year Emperor Zhuangzong pacified Hebei; Shi Jiantang took Xinxiang, and Jingyi paid a visit.

entries.zh: 是歲，上遣使迎至魏州，置北京留守判官承製拜工部尚書，奉使王鎔。
entries.en: That year the emperor sent envoys to bring him to Weizhou, named him investigating officer of the northern capital with imperial commission, appointed him Minister of Works, and sent him as envoy to Wang Rong.
entries.literal: That year the emperor sent envoys to welcome him to Weizhou, appointed him acting northern capital guardian investigating officer with imperial commission, appointed him Minister of Works, and sent him as envoy to Wang Rong.

entries.zh: 敬義以遠祖趙郡，見鎔展維桑之敬，鎔遣判官李翥送《讚皇集》三卷，令謁前代碑壟，使還，歸職太原。
entries.en: Because Jingyi's distant ancestors were of Zhao commandery, when he met Rong he displayed the courtesy due a fellow townsman; Rong sent his aide Li Zhu with three juan of the Zanhuang Collection and had him visit the family tombs and steles of earlier generations. When the mission ended, Jingyi returned to duty at Taiyuan.
entries.literal: Jingyi, because his remote ancestors were of Zhao commandery, when he met Rong displayed hometown respect; Rong sent his aide Li Zhu with three juan of the Zanhuang Collection, ordering him to visit the tombs and steles of former generations. When the envoy returned, Jingyi resumed duty at Taiyuan.

entries.zh: 監軍張承業尤不悅本朝宰輔子孫，待敬義甚薄，或面折於公宴，或指言德裕過惡，敬義不得志，鬱憤而卒。
entries.en: The eunuch commander Zhang Chengye especially disliked descendants of Tang chief ministers and treated Jingyi harshly, sometimes humiliating him at public feasts or reciting Li Deyu's faults; Jingyi failed to prosper and died of grief and anger.
entries.literal: Supervising commander Zhang Chengye especially disliked descendants of this dynasty's chief ministers and treated Jingyi very coldly, sometimes rebuking him to his face at public banquets or pointing out Deyu's faults and crimes; Jingyi could not achieve his aims and died of depressed anger.

entries.zh: 同光二年，贈右僕射。
entries.en: In Tongguang year two he was posthumously honored as Right Vice Director.
entries.literal: In the second year of Tongguang he was posthumously honored as Right Vice Director.

entries.zh: 〈（《五代史闕文》：司空圖，字表聖，自言泗州人。
entries.en: (Lost Texts of the History of the Five Dynasties: Sikong Tu, style name Biaosheng, said he was from Sizhou.
entries.literal: (Lost Texts of the History of the Five Dynasties: Sikong Tu, style name Biaosheng, said himself to be a man of Sizhou.

entries.zh: 少有俊才，威通中，一舉登進士第。
entries.en: He showed outstanding talent in youth and passed the jinshi examination at one sitting in the Xiantong reign.
entries.literal: In youth he had outstanding talent; in the Xiantong era he passed the jinshi examination in a single attempt.

entries.zh: 雅好為文，躁於進取，頗臬矜伐，端士鄙之。
entries.en: He loved literature, was impatient for advancement, rather vain and boastful, and upright gentlemen despised him for it.
entries.literal: He elegantly loved writing, was restless in seeking advancement, rather proud and boastful, and upright gentlemen despised him.

entries.zh: 初，從事使府，及登朝，驟曆清要。
entries.en: He first served in provincial staffs; once he reached court he rose swiftly through the most coveted offices.
entries.literal: At first he served in military commissioners' offices; once he entered court he swiftly passed through pure and important posts.

entries.zh: 巢賊之亂，車駕播遷，圖有先人舊業在中條山，極林泉之美，圖自禮部員外郎，因避地焉，日以詩酒自娛。
entries.en: During Huang Chao's rebellion the court fled; Tu held his family's old estate on Mount Zhongtiao, famed for forest and spring. As Vice Director of Rites he took refuge there and passed his days in poetry and wine.
entries.literal: In the Huang Chao rebellion the imperial carriage was driven abroad; Tu had his forebears' old estate on Mount Zhongtiao, where forests and springs were supremely beautiful. Tu, from his post as Vice Director in the Ministry of Rites, took refuge there and daily amused himself with poetry and wine.

entries.zh: 屬天下板蕩，士多往依之，互相推獎，由是聲名藉甚。
entries.en: With the realm in turmoil, scholars flocked to him and praised one another, and his fame spread far.
entries.literal: As the realm was in turmoil, many scholars went to rely on him and praised one another; because of this his fame spread greatly.

entries.zh: 昭宗反正，以戶部侍郎征至京師。
entries.en: When Emperor Zhaozong restored order, Tu was summoned to the capital as Vice Minister of Revenue.
entries.literal: When Emperor Zhaozong restored order, he was summoned to the capital as Vice Minister of Revenue.

entries.zh: 圖既負才慢世，謂己當為宰輔，時要惡之，稍抑其銳，圖憤憤謝病，復歸中條。
entries.en: Tu, proud of his talent and scornful of the age, believed he should be chief minister; the powerful disliked him and checked his rise. Indignant, he pleaded illness and returned to Mount Zhongtiao.
entries.literal: Tu, relying on his talent and scorning the age, thought he ought to be chief minister; men in power disliked him and slightly checked his edge. Tu indignantly pleaded illness and returned again to Zhongtiao.

entries.zh: 與人書疏，不名官位，但稱知非子，又稱耐辱居士。
entries.en: In correspondence he never used his titles, signing only as Master Who Knows His Faults or Recluse Who Endures Insult.
entries.literal: In letters to others he did not name his office but only called himself Master Who Knows His Faults, and also Recluse Who Endures Insult.

entries.zh: 其所居曰禎貽溪，溪上結茅屋，命曰休休亭，常自為記雲。
entries.en: His home lay on Zhenyi Stream; above the water he built a thatched hut called the Rest-Rest Pavilion and often wrote accounts of it himself.
entries.literal: His dwelling was called Zhenyi Stream; above the stream he built a thatched hut and named it the Rest-Rest Pavilion, often writing his own record of it.

entries.zh: 臣謹案：圖，河中虞鄉人，少有文彩，未為鄉里所稱。
entries.en: Your subject notes: Tu came from Yuxiang in Hezhong; as a youth he showed literary promise but won no praise at home.
entries.literal: Your subject respectfully notes: Tu was a man of Yuxiang in Hezhong; in youth he had literary color but was not praised in his home district.

entries.zh: 會王凝自尚書郎出為絳刺史，圖以文謁之，大為凝所賞歎，由是知名。
entries.en: When Wang Ning left the Secretariat to become prefect of Jiang, Tu presented his writings and won Ning's warm admiration, and from that gained his name.
entries.literal: It happened that Wang Ning went out from a Secretariat post to be prefect of Jiang; Tu presented writings to him and was greatly admired and praised by Ning, and from this became known.

entries.zh: 未幾，凝入知制誥，遷中書舍人、知貢舉。
entries.en: Soon Ning entered the edict office, became Secretariat Drafter, and took charge of the civil examinations.
entries.literal: Before long Ning entered to manage edicts, was transferred to Secretariat Drafter and placed in charge of the examinations.

entries.zh: 擢圖上第。
entries.en: He placed Tu at the head of the list.
entries.literal: He placed Tu in the top rank.

entries.zh: 頃之，凝出為宣州觀察使，辟圖為從事。
entries.en: Before long Ning became surveillance commissioner of Xuanzhou and recruited Tu as an aide.
entries.literal: Shortly after, Ning went out as surveillance commissioner of Xuanzhou and recruited Tu as an aide.

entries.zh: 既渡江，御史府奏圖監察，下詔追之。
entries.en: After he crossed the Yangzi, the Censorate nominated him as investigating censor and the court issued a recall.
entries.literal: After he crossed the river, the Censorate memorialized Tu as Investigating Censor and an edict was issued to recall him.

entries.zh: 圖感知己之恩，不忍輕離幕府，滿百日不赴闕，為台司所劾，遂以本官分司。
entries.en: Grateful to his patron, Tu could not bear to leave the staff; he failed to report within the hundred-day limit and was impeached by the Censorate, serving out his term as a detached official.
entries.literal: Tu, feeling his patron's kindness, could not bear lightly to leave the staff office; a full hundred days he did not attend court and was impeached by the Censorate, and thus served in his original rank as a detached official.

entries.zh: 久之，征拜禮部員外郎，俄知制誥，故集中有文曰：戀恩稽命，點係洛師，於今十年，方忝綸閣，此豈躁於進取者耶！
entries.en: Long afterward he was summoned as Vice Director of Rites and soon managed edicts; his collected works include the line, "Cherishing kindness I delayed my commission, was posted to Luoyang, and only after ten years reached the edict office—was that the conduct of a man restless for office?"
entries.literal: After a long time he was summoned and appointed Vice Director in the Ministry of Rites, and soon managed edicts; hence in his collected works there is a text saying: "Cherishing kindness I delayed my commission, was posted to the Luo capital, and only after ten years did I receive the silk pavilion—how is this one restless in seeking advancement!"

entries.zh: 舊史不詳，一至於此。
entries.en: The old histories omit these details, yet the facts run so far as this.
entries.literal: The old histories are not detailed, yet matters go so far as this.

entries.zh: 圖見唐政多僻，中官用事，知天下必亂，即棄官歸中條山。
entries.en: Tu saw Tang government growing corrupt and eunuchs in power; knowing chaos must come, he resigned at once and returned to Mount Zhongtiao.
entries.literal: Tu saw that Tang government was much perverse and eunuchs held power; knowing the realm must fall into disorder, he immediately abandoned office and returned to Mount Zhongtiao.

entries.zh: 尋以中書舍人征，又拜禮部、戶部侍郎，皆不起。
entries.en: He was soon summoned as Secretariat Drafter and offered the vice ministries of Rites and Revenue, but accepted none of them.
entries.literal: Soon he was summoned as Secretariat Drafter, and again appointed Vice Minister of Rites and Vice Minister of Revenue—all of which he did not accept.

entries.zh: 及昭宗播遷華下，圖以密邇乘輿，即時奔問，復辭還山，故詩曰「多病形容五十三，誰憐借笏趙朝參」，此豈有意於相位耶！
entries.en: When Zhaozong fled to the region below Mount Hua, Tu, living nearby, hurried to pay his respects, then declined and returned to the hills. His poem runs, "Sick at fifty-three, who pities the court attendant clutching his tablet?"—could that be ambition for the chief ministership!
entries.literal: When Emperor Zhaozong was driven abroad below Hua, Tu, because he was near the imperial carriage, at once hurried to inquire after him, then declined and returned to the mountains; hence his poem says, "Sick in many ways, my form at fifty-three—who pities the court attendant borrowing his tablet?"—how could this show intent toward the chief ministership!

entries.zh: 河中節度使王重榮請圖撰碑，得絹數千匹，圖致於虞鄉市心，恣鄉人所取，一日而盡。
entries.en: Wang Chongrong of Hezhong asked Tu to write a stele and paid him several thousand bolts of silk; Tu piled them in the Yuxiang market and let the townspeople take what they wished—it was all gone in a day.
entries.literal: Wang Chongrong, military commissioner of Hezhong, asked Tu to compose a stele inscription and received several thousand bolts of silk; Tu placed them in the market center of Yuxiang and let the villagers take as they pleased—all was gone in a day.

entries.zh: 是時盜賊充斥，獨不入王官穀，河中士人依圖避難，全者甚眾。
entries.en: Bandits filled the land, yet none entered Wangguan Valley; scholars of Hezhong sheltered with Tu, and a great many were spared.
entries.literal: At that time bandits filled the land, yet none entered Wangguan Valley; scholars of Hezhong relied on Tu to avoid disaster, and very many were preserved.

entries.zh: 昭宗東遷，又以兵部侍郎召至洛下，為柳璨所阻，一謝而退。
entries.en: When Zhaozong moved east, Tu was again summoned as Vice Minister of War to Luoyang; Liu Can blocked him, and after a single refusal he withdrew.
entries.literal: When Emperor Zhaozong moved east, he was again summoned as Vice Minister of War to Luoyang, was blocked by Liu Can, declined once and withdrew.

entries.zh: 梁祖受禪，以禮部尚書征，辭以老疾，卒時年八十餘。
entries.en: When the Liang Founder took the throne, Tu was summoned as Minister of Rites; he declined on grounds of age and illness and died in his eighties.
entries.literal: When the Liang Founder received the abdication, he was summoned as Minister of Rites; Tu declined on grounds of age and illness and died at more than eighty years.

entries.zh: 臣又案：梁室大臣，如敬翔、李振、杜曉、楊涉等，皆唐朝舊族，本當忠義立身，重侯累將，三百餘年，一旦委質朱梁，其甚者讚成弑逆。
entries.en: Your subject further notes: Liang ministers such as Jing Xiang, Li Zhen, Du Xiao, and Yang She were old Tang families who should have lived by loyalty; for three hundred years their houses had been enfeoffed and their sons had held command—yet in a day they submitted to Zhu Liang, and the worst praised regicide.
entries.literal: Your subject further notes: great ministers of Liang, such as Jing Xiang, Li Zhen, Du Xiao, and Yang She, were all old clans of Tang and ought originally to have stood in loyalty and righteousness; heavy marquisates and successive generals for more than three hundred years—yet in a single day they submitted to Zhu Liang, and the worst praised and completed regicide.

entries.zh: 惟圖以清直避世，終身不事梁祖，故《梁史》揭圖小瑕以泯大節者，良有以也。）〉
entries.en: Only Tu, through purity and integrity, withdrew from the world and never served the Liang Founder; the Liang History's harping on his small faults to obscure his great integrity is understandable.)〉
entries.literal: Only Tu, through purity and uprightness, avoided the world and all his life did not serve the Liang Founder; therefore the Liang History's raising small flaws of Tu to obscure his great integrity has its reasons.)〉

entries.zh: 盧汝弼，
entries.en: Lu Rubi,
entries.literal: Lu Rubi,

entries.zh: 〈（《宣和書譜》：汝弼字子諧，祖綸，唐貞元年有詩名。
entries.en: (Xuanhe Calligraphy Catalogue: Rubi, style name Zixie; his grandfather Lun was famed for poetry in the Zhenyuan reign.
entries.literal: (Xuanhe Calligraphy Catalogue: Rubi, style name Zixie; his grandfather Lun was famed for poetry in the Zhenyuan era of Tang.

entries.zh: 父簡求，為河東節度使。
entries.en: His father Jianqiu was military commissioner of Hedong.
entries.literal: His father Jianqiu was military commissioner of Hedong.

entries.zh: 汝弼少力學，不喜為世胄，篤誌科舉，登進士第，文彩秀麗，一時士大夫稱之。）〉
entries.en: Rubi studied hard in youth, disdained resting on his birth, devoted himself to the examinations, passed the jinshi, and won praise from contemporaries for his elegant prose.)〉
entries.literal: Rubi in youth studied hard, disliked being a hereditary noble, was devoted to the examinations, passed the jinshi degree, and his literary color was elegant and beautiful—men of the gentry of the time praised him.)〉

entries.zh: 唐昭宗景福中，擢進士第，曆台省。
entries.en: In Emperor Zhaozong's Jingfu reign he passed the jinshi and served in the Censorate and Secretariat.
entries.literal: In the Jingfu era of Emperor Zhaozong of Tang he passed the jinshi and served in the Censorate and Secretariat.

entries.zh: 昭宗自秦遷洛，時為祠部郎中、知制誥。
entries.en: When Zhaozong moved the capital from Qin to Luoyang, Rubi was Director in the Bureau of Sacrifices and managed edicts.
entries.literal: When Emperor Zhaozong moved from Qin to Luo, he was at the time Director in the Bureau of Sacrifices and managed edicts.

entries.zh: 時梁祖淩弱唐室，殄滅衣冠，懼禍渡河，由上黨歸於晉陽。
entries.en: As the Liang Founder bullied the Tang court and destroyed the gentry, Rubi feared for his life, crossed the Yellow River, and from Shangdang made his way to Jinyang.
entries.literal: At the time the Liang Founder bullied and weakened the Tang house and extinguished the gentry; fearing disaster he crossed the river and from Shangdang returned to Jinyang.

entries.zh: 初，武皇平王行瑜，天子許承製授將吏官秩。
entries.en: When the Martial Emperor pacified Wang Xingyu, the emperor allowed him to commission ranks for his officers by imperial order.
entries.literal: At first, when the Martial Emperor pacified Wang Xingyu, the Son of Heaven permitted him to grant officers and clerks ranks by imperial commission.

entries.zh: 是時藩侯倔強者，多偽行墨製，武皇恥而不行，長吏皆表授。
entries.en: Stubborn regional lords then forged written commissions at will; the Martial Emperor disdained that practice and appointed all senior officers by formal memorial.
entries.literal: At that time stubborn feudal lords mostly falsely issued written commissions; the Martial Emperor was ashamed and would not do so—all senior officers were appointed by memorial.

entries.zh: 及莊宗嗣晉王位，承製置吏，又得汝弼，有若符契，由是除補之命，皆出汝弼之手，既而畿內官吏，考課議擬，奔走盈門，頗以賄賂聞，士論少之。
entries.en: When Zhuangzong succeeded to the Jin throne, he again gained Rubi, as if by fate; thereafter all appointments passed through Rubi's hands. Soon officials of the capital districts thronged his gate for examination and promotion, and he gained a reputation for taking bribes, which lowered him in gentlemen's eyes.
entries.literal: When Emperor Zhuangzong succeeded to the Prince of Jin's throne, he commissioned officials by imperial order and again obtained Rubi—as if by tally and contract; from this appointments and supplements all came from Rubi's hand. Later, for officials within the capital districts in examination and deliberation, those who hurried to his gate filled it; he was rather known for bribes, and opinion among gentlemen thought less of him.

entries.zh: 洎帝平定趙、魏，汝弼每請謁迎勞，必陳說天命，顒俟中興，帝亦以宰輔期之。
entries.en: When the emperor pacified Zhao and Wei, Rubi always sought audience to welcome him and expounded the Mandate of Heaven, looking earnestly for restoration; the emperor likewise expected to make him chief minister.
entries.literal: By the time the emperor pacified Zhao and Wei, whenever Rubi requested audience to welcome and comfort him he always expounded the Mandate of Heaven and looked earnestly for restoration; the emperor also expected him for chief minister.

entries.zh: 建國前，卒於晉。
entries.en: He died in Jin before the founding of the dynasty.
entries.literal: Before the founding of the state he died at Jin.

entries.zh: 〈（《宣和書譜》：贈兵部尚書。）〉
entries.en: (Xuanhe Calligraphy Catalogue: posthumously honored as Minister of War.)〉
entries.literal: (Xuanhe Calligraphy Catalogue: posthumously honored as Minister of War.)〉

entries.zh: 蘇循，父特，陳州刺史。
entries.en: Su Xun's father Te was prefect of Chen.
entries.literal: Su Xun—his father Te was prefect of Chen.

entries.zh: 循，咸通中登進士第，累曆台閣。
entries.en: Xun passed the jinshi in the Xiantong reign and rose through the Censorate and Secretariat.
entries.literal: Xun passed the jinshi in the Xiantong era and repeatedly served in the Censorate and Secretariat.

entries.zh: 昭宗朝，再至禮部尚書。
entries.en: Under Emperor Zhaozong he twice served as Minister of Rites.
entries.literal: In the reign of Emperor Zhaozong he twice reached the post of Minister of Rites.

entries.zh: 循性阿諛，善承順苟容，以希進取。
entries.en: Xun was fawning by nature, skilled at compliance and accommodation, and eager for advancement.
entries.literal: Xun's nature was fawning and flattering; he was skilled at complying and accommodating to seek advancement.

entries.zh: 昭宗自遷洛之後，梁祖凶勢日滋，唐室舊臣，陰懷主辱之憤，名族之胄，往往有違禍不仕者，唯循希旨附會。
entries.en: After Zhaozong moved to Luoyang, the Liang Founder's power grew daily; old Tang ministers nursed secret shame for their sovereign's humiliation, and sons of great families often refused office to avoid disaster—only Xun flattered every whim.
entries.literal: After Emperor Zhaozong moved to Luoyang, the Liang Founder's fierce power grew daily; old ministers of the Tang house secretly harbored anger at their lord's disgrace, and scions of famous clans often defied disaster and refused office—only Xun pleased intent and attached himself.

entries.zh: 及梁祖失律於淮南，西屯於壽春，要少帝欲授九錫。
entries.en: When the Liang Founder suffered setbacks in Huainan and encamped at Shouchun, he pressed the young emperor to grant him the Nine Bestowals.
entries.literal: When the Liang Founder lost discipline in Huainan and encamped west at Shouchun, he wished the young emperor to grant the Nine Bestowals.

entries.zh: 朝臣或議是非，循揚言云：「梁王功業顯大，曆數有歸，朝廷速宜揖讓。」
entries.en: When some courtiers debated the matter, Xun proclaimed aloud, "Prince Liang's achievements are manifest; the mandate has turned to him—the court should yield the throne at once."
entries.literal: Some court ministers debated right and wrong; Xun proclaimed aloud: "Prince Liang's achievements and enterprise are manifest and great; the mandate has its return—the court should quickly yield by bowing."

entries.zh: 當時朝士畏梁祖如虎，罔敢違其言者。
entries.en: Court gentlemen then feared the Liang Founder like a tiger, and none dared contradict him.
entries.literal: At the time court gentlemen feared the Liang Founder like a tiger and none dared oppose his words.

entries.zh: 明年，梁祖逼禪，循為冊禮副使。
entries.en: The next year the Liang Founder forced abdication; Xun served as deputy envoy for the enthronement rites.
entries.literal: The next year the Liang Founder forced the abdication; Xun was deputy envoy for the investiture rites.

entries.zh: 梁祖既受命，宴於元德殿，舉酒曰：「朕夾輔日淺，代德未隆，置朕及此者，群公推崇之意也。」
entries.en: After receiving the Mandate, the Liang Founder feasted in the Hall of Primary Virtue and raised his cup: "I have aided the throne but briefly, and my house's virtue is not yet lofty; I stand here through your lords' promotion."
entries.literal: Once the Liang Founder had received the Mandate, he feasted in the Hall of Primary Virtue and raised his cup, saying: "My days aiding the throne have been short, and the virtue of my house is not yet lofty; that I have been placed here is the intent of you lords in promoting me."

entries.zh: 楊涉、張文蔚慚懼失對，致謝而已。
entries.en: Yang She and Zhang Wenwei, ashamed and afraid, could find no reply and only thanked him.
entries.literal: Yang She and Zhang Wenwei, ashamed and afraid, lost their replies and only offered thanks.

entries.zh: 循與張禕、薛貽矩因盛陳梁祖之德業，應天順人之美。
entries.en: Xun, Zhang Yi, and Xue Yiju thereupon lavishly praised the Liang Founder's virtue and the beauty of his accord with Heaven and the people.
entries.literal: Xun with Zhang Yi and Xue Yiju thereupon lavishly set forth the Liang Founder's virtue and enterprise and the beauty of responding to Heaven and following men.

entries.zh: 循自以奉冊之勞，旦夕望居宰輔，而敬翔惡其為人，謂梁祖曰：「聖祚維新，宜選端士，以鎮風俗。
entries.en: Xun, counting on his service in the enthronement rites, expected soon to become chief minister; but Jing Xiang detested him and told the Liang Founder, "The sacred reign is newly renewed—you should choose upright men to steady the manners of the age.
entries.literal: Xun, considering his labor in presenting the enfeoffment documents, morning and evening looked to occupy the chief ministry; but Jing Xiang detested his character and said to the Liang Founder: "The sacred reign is newly renewed—it is fitting to select upright gentlemen to steady custom and teaching.

entries.zh: 如循等輩，俱無士行，實唐家之鴟梟，當今之狐魅，彼專賣國以取利，不可立維新之朝。」
entries.en: Men like Xun lack the conduct of gentlemen; they are Tang's owls and bats, the fox-spirits of our age—men who sell the state for profit cannot build a renewed court."
entries.literal: Men like Xun and his kind all lack the conduct of gentlemen; they are in truth Tang's owl and bat, the fox-spirits of the present age—those who specialize in selling the state for profit cannot establish a renewed court."

entries.zh: 史臣曰：昔武皇之樹霸基，莊宗之開帝業，皆旁求多士，用佐丕圖。
entries.en: The historiographer writes: When the Martial Emperor laid the foundations of hegemony and Zhuangzong opened the imperial enterprise, both sought scholars broadly to assist their great designs.
entries.literal: The historiographer says: In the past, when the Martial Emperor planted the foundation of hegemony and Emperor Zhuangzong opened the imperial enterprise, both broadly sought many scholars to assist their great designs.

entries.zh: 故數君子者，或以書檄敏才，或以搢紳舊族，鹹登貴仕，諒亦宜哉！
entries.en: These gentlemen, whether by nimble pen in letters and proclamations or by birth in old gentry families, all rose to high office—and rightly so!
entries.literal: Therefore these several gentlemen, whether by nimble talent in letters and proclamations or by gentry of old clans, all ascended to exalted office—surely this was fitting!

entries.zh: 唯蘇循讚梁祖之強禪，蘇楷駁昭宗之舊諡，士風臣節，豈若是乎！
entries.en: Only Su Xun praised the Liang Founder's forced abdication and Su Kai rejected Zhaozong's posthumous title—can scholarly integrity and ministerial duty sink so low!
entries.literal: Only Su Xun praised the Liang Founder's forced abdication and Su Kai rejected Emperor Zhaozong's old posthumous title—can scholar custom and ministerial integrity be like this!

entries.zh: 斯蓋文苑之豺狼，儒林之荊棘也。
entries.en: They are jackals and wolves in the grove of letters, thorns in the forest of scholars.
entries.literal: These are jackals and wolves of the literary grove, thorns and brambles of the Confucian forest.

entries.zh: 安元信，字子言，代北人。
entries.en: An Yuanxin, whose style was Ziyan, came from northern Dai.
entries.literal: An Yuanxin, style Ziyan, was a man of northern Dai.

entries.zh: 父順琳，為降野軍使。
entries.en: His father Shunlin served as commander of the Jiangye garrison.
entries.literal: His father Shunlin was commissioner of the Jiangye army.

entries.zh: 元信以將族子，便騎射，幼事武皇，從平巢、蔡。
entries.en: Born into a military family, he was adept at horsemanship and archery and entered the Martial Emperor's service young, fighting through the campaigns against Huang Chao and Qin Zongquan.
entries.literal: Yuanxin, as a son of a general's clan, was skilled at riding and shooting; in youth he served the Martial Emperor and followed the pacification of Huang Chao and Cai.

entries.zh: 光啟中，吐渾赫連鐸寇雲中，武皇使元信拒之，元信兵敗於居庸關。
entries.en: During Guangqi the Tuyuhun chieftain Helian Duo raided Yunzhong; the Martial Emperor sent Yuanxin against him, and Yuanxin was defeated at Juyong Pass.
entries.literal: In the Guangqi era the Tuyuhun Helian Duo raided Yunzhong; the Martial Emperor sent Yuanxin to resist him, and Yuanxin's army was defeated at Juyong Pass.

entries.zh: 武皇性嚴急，元信不敢還，遂奔定州；
entries.en: The Martial Emperor was severe; Yuanxin did not dare go back and fled to Dingzhou.
entries.literal: The Martial Emperor was stern and harsh by nature; Yuanxin dared not return and therefore fled to Dingzhou;

entries.zh: 王處存待之甚厚，用為突騎都校。
entries.en: Wang Chucun received him warmly and made him commander of the shock cavalry.
entries.literal: Wang Chucun treated him very generously and employed him as commander of the shock cavalry.

entries.zh: 乾寧中，處存子郜嗣位。
entries.en: During Qianning, Chucun's son Gao succeeded him.
entries.literal: In the Qianning era Chucun's son Gao succeeded to the post.

entries.zh: 時梁軍攻河朔三鎮，奔命不暇，梁將張存敬軍奄至城下，既無宿備，郜懼，挈其族奔太原，元信從之；
entries.en: The Liang were pressing the three Hebei circuits and Gao had no time to prepare when Zhang Cunjing's army appeared before the walls. In fear Gao took his family to Taiyuan, and Yuanxin went with him.
entries.literal: At the time the Liang army attacked the three Hebei circuits and they had no respite from urgent calls; the Liang general Zhang Cunjing's army suddenly reached the walls. With no prior preparations, Gao was afraid, took his clan and fled to Taiyuan, and Yuanxin followed;

entries.zh: 武皇待之如初，用為鐵林軍使。
entries.en: The Martial Emperor welcomed him as before and appointed him commander of the Iron Forest guard.
entries.literal: The Martial Emperor treated him as before and employed him as commander of the Iron Forest army.

entries.zh: 梁將氏叔琮之攻河東也，別將葛從周自馬嶺入，元信伏於榆次，挫其前鋒。
entries.en: When Shi Shucong attacked Hedong and Ge Congzhou came in by Maling, Yuanxin ambushed him at Yuci and broke his leading columns.
entries.literal: When the Liang general Shi Shucong attacked Hedong, the separate commander Ge Congzhou entered by Maling; Yuanxin lay in ambush at Yuci and checked his vanguard.

entries.zh: 梁將李思安之攻上黨也，王師將壁高河，為梁軍所逼。
entries.en: When Li Si'an of Liang attacked Shangdang, the Jin army was trying to hold Gaohe but was hard pressed by Liang forces.
entries.literal: When the Liang general Li Si'an attacked Shangdang, the royal army was about to entrench at Gaohe but was pressed by the Liang army.

entries.zh: 別將秦武者，尤為難敵，元信與鬥，斃之。
entries.en: Their subordinate Qin Wu was a formidable opponent; Yuanxin met him in combat and killed him.
entries.literal: The separate commander Qin Wu was especially hard to oppose; Yuanxin fought him and killed him.

entries.zh: 由是梁軍解去，城壘得立。
entries.en: The Liang army then withdrew, and the defenses held.
entries.literal: Thereby the Liang army dispersed and left, and the walls and ramparts were secured.

entries.zh: 武皇賜所乘馬及細鎧仗，遷突陣都將。
entries.en: The Martial Emperor gave him his own mount, fine armor, and arms, and promoted him to commander of the assault corps.
entries.literal: The Martial Emperor bestowed the horse he himself rode and fine armor and weapons, and promoted him to commander of the assault formation.

entries.zh: 莊宗嗣晉王位，元信從救上黨，破夾寨，復澤、潞，以功授檢校司空、遼州刺史，賜玉鞭名馬。
entries.en: When Zhuangzong succeeded to the Jin throne, Yuanxin joined the relief of Shangdang, broke the encircling camps, and recovered Ze and Lu; he was made acting Minister of Works and prefect of Liao, and received a jade whip and a celebrated horse.
entries.literal: When Emperor Zhuangzong succeeded to the Jin throne, Yuanxin followed the relief of Shangdang, broke the encircling camps, and recovered Ze and Lu; for merit he was appointed acting Minister of Works and prefect of Liaozhou, and was given a jade whip and a famous horse.

entries.zh: 柏鄉之役，日晚戰酣，元信重傷，莊宗自臨傅藥。
entries.en: At Baixiang, as dusk fell and the fighting raged, Yuanxin was badly wounded; Zhuangzong came in person to dress his wounds.
entries.literal: At the battle of Baixiang, as evening came the fighting grew fierce; Yuanxin was gravely wounded, and Emperor Zhuangzong personally came to apply medicine.

entries.zh: 其年，改檢校司徒、武州刺史，充內衙副都指揮使、山北諸州都團練副使。
entries.en: That same year he was made acting Minister of Education and prefect of Wu, with the posts of deputy commander of the inner guard and deputy overseer of the northern circuits.
entries.literal: That year he was changed to acting Minister of Education and prefect of Wuzhou, and served as deputy commander of the inner palace guard and deputy overseer of training for all circuits north of the mountains.

entries.zh: 從莊宗定魏博，移為博州刺史。
entries.en: He followed Zhuangzong in pacifying Weibo and was transferred to prefect of Bo.
entries.literal: He followed Emperor Zhuangzong in pacifying Weibo and was transferred to be prefect of Bozhou.

entries.zh: 與梁對壘德勝渡，元信為右廂排陣使。
entries.en: When the armies faced each other at Desheng Ford, Yuanxin commanded the right wing in battle order.
entries.literal: Facing Liang across Desheng Ford, Yuanxin was right-wing battle-array officer.

entries.zh: 未幾，為大同軍節度使。
entries.en: Soon afterward he was made commissioner of the Datong circuit.
entries.literal: Before long he became military commissioner of the Datong army.

entries.zh: 莊宗平定河南，移授橫海軍節度使。
entries.en: After Zhuangzong pacified Henan, Yuanxin was transferred and made military commissioner of the Henghai Army.
entries.literal: When Emperor Zhuangzong pacified Henan, he was transferred and appointed military commissioner of the Henghai army.

entries.zh: 時契丹犯邊，元信與霍彥威從明宗屯常山。
entries.en: When the Khitan raided the border, Yuanxin and Huo Yanwei campaigned with Mingzong at Changshan.
entries.literal: At the time the Khitan raided the frontier; Yuanxin and Huo Yanwei followed Emperor Mingzong in encamping at Changshan.

entries.zh: 元信恃功，每對明宗以成敗勇怯戲侮彥威，彥威不敢答。
entries.en: Yuanxin, proud of his record, would bait Yanwei before Mingzong with jibes about who had won or lost and who was brave or timid; Yanwei never answered back.
entries.literal: Yuanxin relied on his merit and, in Emperor Mingzong's presence, would mock Yanwei with talk of victory and defeat, courage and cowardice; Yanwei dared not reply.

entries.zh: 明宗曰：「成由天地，不由於人。
entries.en: Mingzong said, "Victory belongs to Heaven and earth, not to any man.
entries.literal: Emperor Mingzong said: "Success lies with Heaven and Earth, not with men.

entries.zh: 當氏叔琮圍太原，公有何勇！
entries.en: When Shi Shucong besieged Taiyuan, what courage did you show then!
entries.literal: When Shi Shucong besieged Taiyuan, what courage did you have!

entries.zh: 今國家運興，致我等富貴。」
entries.en: It is the dynasty's rising fortune that has made us rich and honored."
entries.literal: Now the state's fortune rises and has brought us wealth and rank."

entries.zh: 勿以小勝小捷掛於口吻，取笑於長者。
entries.en: Do not parade petty triumphs in your speech and make a laughingstock of yourself before your seniors.
entries.literal: Do not hang small victories and small successes on your lips and make sport of your elders.

entries.zh: 元信乃起謝，不復以彥威為戲。
entries.en: Yuanxin rose to apologize and never again mocked Yanwei.
entries.literal: Yuanxin then rose and apologized and no longer made sport of Yanwei.

entries.zh: 明宗即位，以元信嘗為內衙都校，尤厚待之，加同中書門下平章事。
entries.en: When Mingzong came to the throne he treated Yuanxin with exceptional favor because they had served together in the inner guard, and made him Associate Grand Councillor.
entries.literal: When Emperor Mingzong took the throne, because Yuanxin had once been chief of the inner palace guard he treated him with special favor and added the title Associate Grand Councillor of the Secretariat and Chancellery.

entries.zh: 明年，移鎮徐州。
entries.en: The following year he was transferred to Xuzhou.
entries.literal: The next year he was transferred to garrison Xuzhou.

entries.zh: 王師之討高季興，襄帥劉訓逗撓軍期，移授元信山南東道節度使以代訓。
entries.en: During the campaign against Gao Jixing, the Xiang commander Liu Xun dragged his feet; Yuanxin was made commissioner of Shannan East to replace him.
entries.literal: When the royal army attacked Gao Jixing, the Xiang military commissioner Liu Xun dallied and delayed the campaign schedule; Yuanxin was transferred and appointed military commissioner of the Shannan East circuit to replace Xun.

entries.zh: 歲餘，改歸德軍節度使，就加兼侍中。
entries.en: A year later he was transferred to commissioner of Guide and concurrently made Palace Attendant.
entries.literal: After more than a year he was changed to military commissioner of the Guide army and was at the same time additionally made Palace Attendant.

entries.zh: 明宗不豫，求入。
entries.en: When Mingzong fell ill, he asked to return to court.
entries.literal: When Emperor Mingzong fell ill, he requested to enter the capital.

entries.zh: 末帝即位，授潞州節度使，加檢校太尉。
entries.en: When the Last Emperor succeeded, Yuanxin was made commissioner of Lu and acting Grand Commandant.
entries.literal: When the Last Emperor took the throne, he was appointed military commissioner of Luzhou and added acting Grand Commandant.

entries.zh: 清泰三年二月，以疾卒於鎮，時年七十四。
entries.en: In the second month of Qingtai 3 he died of illness at his post, aged seventy-four.
entries.literal: In the second month of the third year of Qingtai he died of illness in his commission; he was then seventy-four.

entries.zh: 贈太師。
entries.en: The court posthumously enfeoffed him as Grand Preceptor.
entries.literal: He was posthumously enfeoffed as Grand Preceptor.

entries.zh: 晉高祖即位，以元信宿望，令禮官定諡曰忠懿。
entries.en: When the Jin founder Gaozu came to the throne, he honored Yuanxin's long service by having the ritual officers confer the posthumous name Loyal and Admirable.
entries.literal: When Emperor Gaozu of Jin took the throne, because of Yuanxin's long-standing repute he ordered the ritual officers to fix his posthumous title as Loyal and Admirable.

entries.zh: 劉訓，字遵範，隰州永和人也。
entries.en: Liu Xun, whose style was Zunfan, came from Yonghe in Xi prefecture.
entries.literal: Liu Xun, style Zunfan, was a native of Yonghe in Xizhou.

entries.zh: 出身行間，初事武皇為馬軍隊長，漸至散將。
entries.en: He rose through the ranks, first serving the Martial Emperor as a cavalry captain and eventually becoming a field general.
entries.literal: He rose from the ranks; at first he served the Martial Emperor as captain of the horse army and gradually reached the post of irregular general.

entries.zh: 屬河中王氏昆仲有尋戈之役，訓從史儼攻陝州。
entries.en: During the civil war among the Wang brothers of Hezhong, Xun followed Shi Yan in the attack on Shanzhou.
entries.literal: When the Wang brothers of Hezhong had their fraternal strife, Xun followed Shi Yan in attacking Shanzhou.

entries.zh: 武皇討王行瑜，以訓為前鋒，後隸河中，為隰州防禦都將。
entries.en: When the Martial Emperor campaigned against Wang Xingyu, Xun led the van; he later entered Hezhong service as defense commander of Xi.
entries.literal: The Martial Emperor campaigned against Wang Xingyu and made Xun vanguard; later he was attached to Hezhong as defense commander of Xizhou.

entries.zh: 居無何，殺陝州刺史，以郡歸莊宗，曆瀛州刺史。
entries.en: Soon he killed the prefect of Shan, surrendered the commandery to Zhuangzong, and later served as prefect of Ying.
entries.literal: After a short time he killed the prefect of Shanzhou, surrendered the commandery to Emperor Zhuangzong, and served in turn as prefect of Yingzhou.

entries.zh: 同光初，拜左監衛大將軍。
entries.en: Early in Tongguang he was made great general of the Left Guard.
entries.literal: At the beginning of Tongguang he was appointed great general of the Left Guard.

entries.zh: 三年，授襄州節度使。
entries.en: In the third year he was made commissioner of Xiang.
entries.literal: In the third year he was appointed military commissioner of Xiangzhou.

entries.zh: 四年四月，洛陽有變，訓以私忿害節度副使胡裝，族其家，聞者冤之。
entries.en: In the fourth month of the fourth year, when Luoyang was in turmoil, Xun killed his deputy Hu Zhuang in a private grudge and wiped out Hu's family—a deed widely judged unjust.
entries.literal: In the fourth month of the fourth year there was turmoil in Luoyang; Xun, from private resentment, harmed the deputy military commissioner Hu Zhuang and exterminated his clan; those who heard of it considered it unjust.

entries.zh: 天成中，荊南高季興叛，詔訓為南面行營招討使，知荊南行府事。
entries.en: During Tiancheng, when Gao Jixing of Jingnan rebelled, Xun was appointed southern campaign commander with authority over the Jingnan field headquarters.
entries.literal: In Tiancheng, when Jingnan's Gao Jixing rebelled, Xun was ordered to be southern campaign pacification commissioner and to manage the Jingnan field headquarters.

entries.zh: 是時，湖南馬殷請以舟師會，及王師至荊渚，殷軍方到岳州。
entries.en: Ma Yin of Hunan had offered a naval contingent, but when the imperial army reached Jingzhou his fleet had only just reached Yue.
entries.literal: At that time Hunan's Ma Yin offered to join with a fleet; when the royal army reached Jingzhu, Yin's army had only just arrived at Yuezhou.

entries.zh: 仍傳意於訓，許助軍儲弓甲之類，久之，略無至者。
entries.en: Yin still sent assurances of grain, arms, and armor, yet after a long wait almost nothing came.
entries.literal: He still sent word to Xun promising aid in military stores, bows, armor, and the like, but after a long time virtually nothing arrived.

entries.zh: 〈（案《通鑒》：劉訓至荊南，楚王殷遣都指揮使許德勳等將水軍屯岳州。
entries.en: (Per the 《Zizhi Tongjian》: When Liu Xun reached Jingnan, King Yin of Chu sent Xu Dexun and others with the fleet to encamp at Yue.
entries.literal: (According to the 《Zizhi Tongjian》: When Liu Xun reached Jingnan, King Yin of Chu sent Commander-in-Chief Xu Dexun and others to lead the water army and encamp at Yuezhou.

entries.zh: 高季興堅壁不戰，求救於吳，吳人遣水軍援之。）〉
entries.en: Gao Jixing held his walls and refused battle, begged Wu for help, and Wu sent naval reinforcements.)〉
entries.literal: Gao Jixing held his walls and would not fight, begged aid from Wu, and the Wu sent a water army to reinforce him.) 〉

entries.zh: 荊渚地氣卑濕，漸及霖潦，糧運不繼，人多疾疫。
entries.en: The Jingzhou lowlands were humid; rains and floods followed, supplies failed, and pestilence spread through the army.
entries.literal: The Jingzhu region's air was low and damp; gradually heavy rains and floods came, grain transport could not keep up, and many men fell to pestilence.

entries.zh: 訓本無將略，人鹹苦之。
entries.en: Xun had no talent for command, and the troops suffered under him.
entries.literal: Xun by nature had no military strategy, and all men suffered under him.

entries.zh: 及孔循至，得襄之小校獻竹龍之術，及造竹龍二道，傅於城下，竟無所濟。
entries.en: When Kong Xun came, a junior officer from Xiang offered a "bamboo dragon" siege device; they built two and set them against the walls, but they accomplished nothing.
entries.literal: When Kong Xun arrived, he obtained a junior officer of Xiang who presented the technique of bamboo dragons; they built two bamboo dragons and placed them against the walls, but in the end it availed nothing.

entries.zh: 遂罷兵，令將士散略居民而回。
entries.en: They withdrew the army and let the troops plunder the countryside on the march home.
entries.literal: They then dismissed the army and ordered officers and soldiers to scatter and plunder the inhabitants on the way back.

entries.zh: 詔訓赴闕，尋責授檀州刺史，續敕濮州安置，未幾，起為龍武大將軍，尋授建雄軍節度使，移鎮延平。
entries.en: Xun was recalled to court, demoted to prefect of Tan, then confined at Pu; soon he was restored as Dragon Martial great general, made commissioner of Jianxiong, and transferred to Yanping.
entries.literal: Xun was ordered to the capital; soon he was demoted and appointed prefect of Tanzhou, then further ordered settled at Puzhou. Before long he was raised to great general of the Dragon Martial guard, then appointed military commissioner of the Jianxiong army and transferred to garrison Yanping.

entries.zh: 卒贈太尉。
entries.en: He died and was posthumously enfeoffed as Grand Commandant.
entries.literal: On his death he was posthumously enfeoffed as Grand Commandant.

entries.zh: 西方鄴，定州滿城人也。
entries.en: Xifang Ye came from Mancheng in Ding prefecture.
entries.literal: Xifang Ye was a native of Mancheng in Dingzhou.

entries.zh: 父再遇，為州軍校。
entries.en: His father Zaiyu was a prefectural garrison officer.
entries.literal: His father Zaiyu was a garrison officer of the prefecture.

entries.zh: 鄴居軍中，以勇力聞。
entries.en: Ye grew up in the army and was famed for his strength.
entries.literal: Ye lived in the army and was known for courage and strength.

entries.zh: 年二十，南渡河遊梁，不見用，復歸。
entries.en: At twenty he crossed south to seek service with Liang, found no post, and came home.
entries.literal: At twenty he crossed the river south to seek service in Liang, was not employed, and returned.

entries.zh: 莊宗以為孝義軍指揮使，累從征伐皆有功。
entries.en: Zhuangzong made him commander of the Xiaoyi army, and he distinguished himself in campaign after campaign.
entries.literal: Emperor Zhuangzong made him commander of the Xiaoyi army; he repeatedly followed campaigns and always had merit.

entries.zh: 同光中，為曹州刺史，以州兵屯汴州。
entries.en: During Tongguang he was prefect of Cao and posted his troops at Bian.
entries.literal: In Tongguang he was prefect of Caozhou and stationed the prefectural troops at Bianzhou.

entries.zh: 明宗自魏州，南渡河，時莊宗東幸汴州。
entries.en: Mingzong marched south from Wei while Zhuangzong was traveling east to Bian.
entries.literal: Emperor Mingzong came from Weizhou and crossed the river south; at the time Emperor Zhuangzong was traveling east to Bianzhou.

entries.zh: 汴州節度使孔循懷二誌，使北門迎明宗，西門迎莊宗，所以供帳委積悉如一，曰：「先至者入之。」
entries.en: The Bian commissioner Kong Xun hedged his bets, prepared the north gate for Mingzong and the west gate for Zhuangzong, stocked both equally, and said, "Whoever arrives first may enter."
entries.literal: The Bianzhou military commissioner Kong Xun harbored two intentions, had the north gate receive Mingzong and the west gate receive Zhuangzong, and made all supplies and stores identical, saying: "Whoever arrives first may enter."

entries.zh: 鄴因責循曰：「主上破梁室於公，有不殺之恩，奈何欲納總管而負國？」
entries.en: Ye rebuked him: "Our lord destroyed Liang for your sake and spared your life—how can you welcome the chief commander and betray the throne?"
entries.literal: Ye therefore rebuked Xun: "Our lord destroyed the Liang house for you and showed the grace of not killing you—how can you wish to welcome the chief commander and betray the state?"

entries.zh: 循不答。
entries.en: Xun made no reply.
entries.literal: Xun did not answer.

entries.zh: 鄴度循不可爭，以石敬瑭妻，明宗女也，時方在汴，欲殺之以堅人心。
entries.en: Seeing that Xun would not yield, Ye considered killing Shi Jingtang's wife—the emperor's daughter, then at Bian—to steady loyalty.
entries.literal: Ye judged that Xun could not be argued with; Shi Jingtang's wife, who was Emperor Mingzong's daughter, was then at Bian, and he wished to kill her to steady men's hearts.

entries.zh: 循知其謀，取之藏其家，鄴無如之何。
entries.en: Xun learned of the plan, took her into hiding, and Ye was helpless.
entries.literal: Xun learned of the plot, took her and hid her in his house, and Ye could do nothing.

entries.zh: 而明宗已及汴，乃將麾下兵五百騎西迎莊宗，見於汜水，嗚咽泣下，莊宗亦為之噓唏，使以兵為先鋒。
entries.en: Mingzong had already reached Bian; Ye led five hundred horsemen west to meet Zhuangzong at Sishui, wept before him, and Zhuangzong, moved in turn, made his men the vanguard.
entries.literal: But Mingzong had already reached Bian; Ye then led five hundred horsemen of his command west to welcome Zhuangzong, met him at Sishui, sobbed and wept, and Zhuangzong also sighed for him and had his troops serve as vanguard.

entries.zh: 莊宗至汴西，不得入，還洛陽，遇弑。
entries.en: Zhuangzong reached the west bank of Bian but could not enter, returned to Luoyang, and was murdered.
entries.literal: Zhuangzong reached the west of Bian but could not enter, returned to Luoyang, and met assassination.

entries.zh: 明宗入洛，鄴請死於馬前，明宗嘉歎久之。
entries.en: When Mingzong entered Luoyang, Ye asked to die at his horse's feet; Mingzong praised him at length.
entries.literal: When Mingzong entered Luoyang, Ye asked to die before his horse; Mingzong praised and sighed over him for a long time.

entries.zh: 明年，荊南高季興叛，明宗遣襄州節度使劉訓等招討，而以東川董璋為西南招討使，乃拜鄴夔州刺史，副璋，以兵出三峽。
entries.en: The following year, when Gao Jixing of Jingnan rebelled, Mingzong sent Liu Xun of Xiang and others against him and made Dong Zhang of Dongchuan southwestern commander; Ye was made prefect of Qi to assist Zhang and marched through the Three Gorges.
entries.literal: The next year, when Jingnan's Gao Jixing rebelled, Mingzong sent the Xiang military commissioner Liu Xun and others to pacify him, and made Dongchuan's Dong Zhang southwestern pacification commissioner; Ye was appointed prefect of Qizhou to assist Zhang and led troops out through the Three Gorges.

entries.zh: 已而訓等無功見黜，諸將皆罷，璋未嘗出兵，惟鄴獨取夔、忠、萬三州，乃以夔州為寧江軍，拜鄴節度使。
entries.en: Soon Xun and the others were dismissed for failure; the other generals were recalled and Zhang never marched—only Ye captured Qi, Zhong, and Wan, after which Qi was organized as the Ningjiang circuit and Ye was made its commissioner.
entries.literal: Before long Xun and the others were dismissed without merit; all the generals were relieved, and Zhang never once sent out troops—only Ye alone took Qi, Zhong, and Wan, whereupon Qi was made the Ningjiang army and Ye was appointed military commissioner.

entries.zh: 已而又取歸州，數敗季興之兵。
entries.en: He then took Gui as well and repeatedly defeated Jixing's forces.
entries.literal: Before long he also took Guizhou and repeatedly defeated Jixing's troops.

entries.zh: 鄴，武人，所為多不中法度，判官譚善達數以諫鄴，鄴怒，遣人告善達受人金，下獄。
entries.en: A soldier by trade, Ye often ignored the law; his aide Tan Shanda remonstrated repeatedly until Ye, enraged, had him accused of bribery and thrown into prison.
entries.literal: Ye was a military man whose actions mostly failed to accord with law; his aide Tan Shanda repeatedly remonstrated with him. Ye was angry, sent men to accuse Shanda of taking bribes, and put him in prison.

entries.zh: 善達素剛，辭益不遜，遂死於獄中。
entries.en: Shanda was stubborn by nature and grew only more defiant in speech until he died in prison.
entries.literal: Shanda was by nature stubborn; his words grew ever more insubordinate, and he died in prison.

entries.zh: 鄴病，見善達為祟，卒於鎮。
entries.en: Ye fell ill, was haunted by visions of Shanda, and died at his post.
entries.literal: Ye fell ill, saw Shanda as a haunting spirit, and died in his commission.

entries.zh: 安重霸，雲州人也。
entries.en: An Zhongba came from Yunzhou.
entries.literal: An Zhongba was a man of Yunzhou.

entries.zh: 性狡譎，多智算。
entries.en: He was cunning and full of schemes.
entries.literal: By nature he was crafty and cunning, with much stratagem.

entries.zh: 初，自代北與明宗俱事武皇，因負罪奔梁；
entries.en: He had served the Martial Emperor in northern Dai alongside Mingzong, then fled to Liang after a crime.
entries.literal: At first, from northern Dai he and Emperor Mingzong together served the Martial Emperor; because of a crime he fled to Liang;

entries.zh: 在梁復以罪奔蜀，蜀以蕃人善騎射，因為親將。
entries.en: He fled Liang for Shu on another charge; Shu valued his frontier horsemanship and made him a personal guard.
